title: 🎟️OCC Invite #theatre #broadway #romeoandjuliet #kitconnor #rachelzeg...
transcript: I'm gonna defend this Broadway production of Romeo and Juliet starring Kit Connor and Rachel Zegler for those who haven't already seen it or seen clips circulating on this app the production is done in a way that's designed to feel like an experience from the moment you enter the lobby Through to the end of the show And like yeah I can see a case for calling this production a little bit hollow or vapid but I feel like that slightly misses the point I almost never use this phrase because it kind of goes against my entire brand but Romeo and Juliet I will say: it's actually not that deep and I'd like to think that I know this play pretty well okay this is the fourth version of it that I've seen in 2024 alone and I've seen it many many times before that I was also even in charge of cutting the script for a production that I was in which literally required me to comb through it line by line and I'm not saying this to brag I'm just trying to demonstrate that I'm not saying this lightly like I love this play, I love it dearly and yes it has something to say and yes it's emotionally rich and yes the language is some of the most beautiful that Shakespeare ever wrote I think those things kinda speak for themselves like they kind of exist on the surface level for the most part I feel like some people are talking about Romeo and Juliet like it's Hamlet or King Lear and requires that same level of mining it for depth and by the way I've seen this same director Sam Gold take a similar approach to both of those plays and it did feel hollow But Romeo and Juliet is a play that frankly if you have the right vibe and the right chemistry and pacing it kind of takes you 80% of the way there and 80% is pretty much where I'd put this production like no, it's not the most coherent or emotionally striking rendition of the play that I've seen but it gets the job done I've also heard some people say that this production lacks a sense of poetry but to me it just came across as grounded and comfortable which then translates to a sense of clarity and accessibility and I think for a production that is predominantly aimed at bringing in a new audience I think that's great I do wanna address that you know people are referring to this as like a Gen Z coded production I am curious to hear from Gen Z people if it reads as authentic or whether it has kind of a “how do you do fellow kids” quality to it I have to wonder because it was in fact directed by a 46 year old man I'm a young millennial and I think that put me in a good position to appreciate the production because it's close enough to feel relatable and specific but far enough that I wouldn't necessarily pick up on that “how do you do fellow kids” inauthenticity if in fact there was any to pick up on And I didn't think the production was perfect like not every choice worked for me and like most productions of this play I do think it struggled a bit to navigate the tone shift between the first two acts and the last three acts I also do agree that Kit Connor outshines Rachel Zegler to some extent I actually did think she was good and the two of them have good chemistry but her performance didn't pop to life quite in the way that his did but aside from that the production really worked for me I think this is a play that thrives on a sense of immediacy so this inviting, relatable, interactive quality to the production wasn't just a gimmick to me I think it is very much in conversation with Shakespeare's play
reasoning: The creator defends the production and says it 'really worked for me' despite acknowledging some flaws. They rate it at '80% of the way there' and appreciate its accessibility and chemistry, which signals a positive recommendation with caveats.
